title: Sin Bin Concierge
pitch: You run the penalty box as a tiny, deadpan hotel: guests arrive with minors, double minors, majors and misconducts, goals go in, whistles blow, and you must announce who checks out and what the strength on the ice is, before the clock runs out. A real rules engine decides the right answer, including the awkward cases like coincidental minors, a goal on a stacked kill, and a major that refuses to leave early.
whyNow: Timeless. The 2026-27 NHL season (84 games per team) is under way, and a faithful penalty-clock puzzle is the kind of rule detail fans argue about; it is a humor entry that rewards learning real rules.

research.summary: Hockey penalty expiry is a small state machine. Searches agree that a power-play goal releases the minor with the least time left (NHL.com history piece, IIHF and USA Hockey rule text), that a five-minute major is not cut short by goals (NHL.com glossary), that a double minor is two back-to-back two-minute blocks with a goal ending only the block being served, and that NHL coincidental minors at even strength give four-on-four while IIHF play stays five-on-five (Wikipedia and an IIHF comparison document). The NHL's own current rulebook text was not opened and the IIHF, USA Hockey and walkthrough texts are other bodies' or older, so the page labels the engine a simplified house version of NHL rules. Searches found no reported NHL penalty-rule change for 2026-27; the season is 84 games per team.

facts.claim: The 2026-27 NHL regular season is 84 games per team, the first 84-game season since 1993-94.
A goal by the team on the power play releases a penalized player serving a minor (NHL rule since 1956); the minor with the least time remaining ends first, and a penalty-shot goal does not count.
A five-minute major is not shortened by power-play goals; it runs its full length.
In the NHL, coincidental minors at even strength produce four-on-four play, whereas IIHF rules keep five-on-five.
In a double minor, a power-play goal in the first two minutes ends only the first block, and a goal in the final two minutes ends the power play.

design.coreLoop: A seeded game script produces a timeline of whistles, goals and expiries. At each decision point the concierge sees the box ledger (guest, penalty, clock) and must tap who is released and set the on-ice strength, before a patience meter runs out. The rules engine scores each answer, explains the ruling in one deadpan line, and ramps difficulty by stacking penalties, adding coincidentals, majors, misconducts and goals mid-kill. Shifts are daily-seeded and shareable via URL hash so friends compare rulings.
sophisticationHooks: Pure, tested penalty-clock state machine: queue ordering of simultaneous penalties, double minor block logic, major versus minor release on goals, coincidental handling, minimum skater counts
Scenario generator with seeded randomness that guarantees each shift contains specific edge cases at rising difficulty and never an ambiguous ruling
Explanations built from the same rule trace the engine used, so every correct and wrong answer is teachable
Absurd framing: invented guests and teams, a hotel-ledger look drawn in SVG and CSS, keyboard-only play and a replay of the ruling
design.scopeForOneDay: Build the pure penalty-clock engine with a node test file, a seeded scenario generator limited to hand-checked patterns (single and stacked minors, double minor, major, even-strength coincidental minors, power-play goals mid-kill, misconducts as no-strength decoys), the ledger and rink-strength UI, scoring with a patience meter, daily seed and share hash, and an about panel that lists the exact simplified rules. Cut: delayed penalties, coincidental penalties while other penalties are running, penalty shots, overtime, referee signals, audio and per-league variants.
risks: The engine follows rules corroborated by NHL.com pages, IIHF and USA Hockey texts and explainers, but the current NHL rulebook text was not opened: the about panel says simplified house version, as of 2026-10-12, and never claims official rulings.
Coincidental minors with other penalties already on the clock are served differently and were not verified; the generator never produces that case.
Stacked or simultaneous edge cases could yield a disputed answer: the generator is limited to patterns a second pass (test vectors written by hand) agrees on.
Humor can thin once the rules click: vary guest personas and add chained late-night shifts.
Invented guests and teams only; no real names, logos or marks. The claim that penalty-heavy games are in the news was unverified and is removed from the pitch.

verification.notes: Rule claims and the 84-game fact were each seen in two or more independent search results (NHL.com, IIHF, USA Hockey, ESPN) but no page opened (DNS failures); unverified news hook removed and scope trimmed to hand-checkable penalty patterns.
